How long is an ice hockey rink built to international measurements?
An NHL rink is a little shorter and clearly narrower, which is why the game there looks more cramped.
What do the two blue lines on an ice hockey rink decide?
The red centre line is the one used for icing; the blue lines mark the three zones.
How wide is an ice hockey goal?
Seventy-two inches of opening, and a goaltender padded out to fill as much of it as the rules allow.
What is unusual about the goalkeeper in floorball?
They may leave the rink during play
They are allowed to score with their hands
They change ends every two minutes
The keeper kneels and catches, which is why the gloves and the knee pads matter more than any stick.
How many holes does a floorball ball have?
Twenty-six holes of ten millimetres each, in a plastic ball weighing just 23 grams.
How long is one period in a standard floorball match?
Three periods of twenty. The sport was organised into leagues in Gothenburg in the 1970s.
Lasse Virén won the same two Olympic running titles at two Games in a row. Which two?
Munich in 1972 and Montreal in 1976, four golds in all.
What happened to Lasse Virén partway through the 1972 Olympic 10,000 metres final?
He stopped to help a rival
He got tangled with another runner around the twelfth lap, got up, caught the field and set a world record.
What is the diameter of a table tennis ball?
The ball was made bigger in 2000, from 38 millimetres, to slow the rallies down for television.
How many points does it take to win a game of table tennis?
If both reach ten the game runs on until someone leads by two.
What is the black ball worth in snooker?
Yellow two, green three, brown four, blue five, pink six, black seven, and a red is worth one.
Once the reds are gone in snooker, which colour has to be potted first?
The colours then go in rising order of value, from the cheapest to the black.
How many obstacles does a runner clear in the men's 3000 metres steeplechase?
Twenty-eight plain barriers and seven with water behind them.
How many water jumps are taken in a 3000 metres steeplechase?
One per lap, plus the first one before the runners settle into the laps.
What is the radius of the centre circle on a football pitch?
Ten yards, converted. The same distance is used for the arc outside the penalty area.
How big is the quarter-circle marked at each corner flag on a football pitch?
The ball has to sit inside that arc for a corner, which is why defenders argue about it.
How high is the crossbar on a full-size football goal?
Eight feet high and eight yards wide, and the posts may be no thicker than twelve centimetres.
How far out from the goal line does a football penalty area reach?
Eighteen yards, which is why English commentators still call it the eighteen-yard box.
How far is the throwing line from the dartboard?
The line is called the oche: seven feet nine and a quarter inches from the face of the board.
How high above the floor is the centre of a dartboard hung?
Five feet eight inches, which was once about the height of an average player's eyes.
What does the ring immediately around the centre of a dartboard score?
The centre itself is fifty, and it also counts as a double when you are finishing a leg.
How must a leg of darts be finished?
With any dart that brings the score to zero
Land on one, or drop below zero, and the whole turn is void: the score goes back to where it started.
In rugby union, how many points does the kick taken after a try add?
The try itself is five, so a converted try is worth seven.
How many points is a drop goal worth in rugby union?
The same as a penalty kick, and it has decided more than one World Cup final.
Which code of rugby is played with thirteen in a team?
Two fewer than union, and the split goes back to a nineteenth-century row about paying players.
What does the polka-dot jersey stand for at the Tour de France?
A climbers' prize has been awarded since 1933, but the jersey itself only arrived in 1975.
Who wears the white jersey at the Tour de France?
The leader of the points competition
The points competition is the green one, and it usually falls to a sprinter.
How heavy is the discus thrown in the men's event?
The women's discus weighs one kilo. The shot, by contrast, weighs the same 7.26 kg as the hammer.
How heavy is the men's javelin?
The women's javelin is 600 grams. The weight is in the rules; the length and balance point are too.
How big is a handball goal?
Small enough that a goalkeeper can reach the corners, and the court is 40 by 20 metres.
How many steps may a handball player take while holding the ball?
Or stand still for three seconds. After that it has to be a pass, a shot or a bounce.
How long are the two halves of a handball match?
An hour of running play, which is why handball scores climb into the thirties.
What served as the first basketball hoops?
They were nailed to the gym balcony rail with their bottoms still in, so the ball had to be fetched out.
How many rules did James Naismith write for his new game in 1891?
The first game was played with a football, in a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Which of these figure skating jumps is named after a Swedish skater?
Axel Paulsen was Norwegian, Alois Lutz Austrian and Werner Rittberger German.
The throwing game kyykkä came originally from which region?
It is centuries older than its small cousin on the summer lawn, and student teams still play it on ice.
How many skittles stand on the field in a team game of kyykkä?
Twenty pairs of them. The individual game uses half as many.
How big is each playing square in kyykkä?
Skittles left inside the square, or sitting on its lines, count against you, so a score can go negative.
How long is a half in swamp football?
Short, because knee-deep peat takes everything out of you. The world championships have run at Hyrynsalmi since 1998.
In which Finnish town are the Mobile Phone Throwing World Championships held?
Thrown since 2000, with a junior class for children of twelve and under.
Apart from plain distance, what is judged in one of the mobile phone throwing classes?
The freestyle class rewards aesthetics and invention; the traditional class is a plain over-the-shoulder throw.
Which nickname grew up around Hannes Kolehmainen and the Finnish distance runners after him?
He took three golds at the 1912 Games and later became an American citizen.
How many Formula 1 world titles did Mika Häkkinen win?
Back to back in 1998 and 1999, both of them with McLaren.
How many clubs may a golfer carry during a round?
Carrying one too many costs two strokes a hole in stroke play, up to a maximum of four.
Which three weapons are used in Olympic fencing?
Each has its own target area and its own rules about who had the right to attack.
In which fencing weapon does the whole body count as a target?
The other two are limited to the body above the waist, so a hit to the foot counts in only one of the three.
How wide is the ring in sumo?
It was briefly widened to 4.85 metres in 1945 and then put back as it had been.
What marks the edge of a sumo ring?
The ring is built up out of clay, and four of the bales are set slightly outside the circle.
How many legal deliveries make up an over in cricket?
Overs of four, five and eight have all been used; wides and no-balls still do not count towards the six.
In which year was the first 24 Hours of Le Mans run?
It began as a Grand Prix of speed and endurance on the public roads of the Sarthe.
Out of which country's military training did orienteering grow?
Land navigation drills in the late nineteenth century turned into a civilian sport, then into a Nordic obsession.
What are the points an orienteer has to visit on the course called?
Each one is punched, electronically these days, which also records how long each leg took.
A bandy field is about the size of which other playing surface?
Roughly a hundred metres by fifty-five, which is why the game is skated rather than fought in the corners.
Which is the highest mountain in Norway?
At 2,469 metres in the Jotunheimen range, it is the highest ground anywhere in the Nordic countries.
Which is the highest mountain in Sweden?
Its northern peak reaches 2,097 metres. The glaciated southern peak was once the taller of the two, but its ice is melting away.
Which mountain is the highest point of Switzerland?
The 4,634-metre peak crowns the Monte Rosa massif. The Matterhorn is far more famous and some 150 metres lower.
Which mountain is the highest point of Poland?
The border with Slovakia runs right over the 2,499-metre mountain, so its true summit is on the Slovak side.
Which mountain is the highest point of Spain?
The 3,718-metre volcano is on Tenerife in the Canaries. Mulhacén, at 3,482 metres, only tops the mainland.
Which mountain is the highest point of Portugal?
The 2,351-metre volcano stands on Pico island in the Azores. The mainland's highest ground is only 1,993 metres.
Which hill is the highest point of all three Baltic states?
The Estonian hill manages 318 metres, six more than the best Latvia can offer and twenty-four more than Lithuania's.
Which mountain is the highest point of the whole Danish realm?
It rises 3,694 metres in eastern Greenland, while the highest ground in Denmark proper is a 171-metre field.
Which is the highest mountain in Antarctica?
Nobody had even seen the 4,892-metre peak until a US navy aircraft flew over it in 1958.
Which mountain is the highest point of Australia?
At 2,228 metres it is the lowest of the seven continental summits — low enough that a walking track reaches the top.
In which country is Puncak Jaya, the highest peak of Oceania?
The 4,884-metre peak is on New Guinea and carries the only glaciers between the Himalayas and the Andes.
In which mountain range does K2 stand?
The world's second highest mountain is not in the Himalayas at all, and kills a far greater share of those who try it.
Which mountain is the highest point of India?
At 8,586 metres it is the world's third highest. Everest belongs to Nepal and China, and K2 to Pakistan.
Which mountain is the highest point of Iran?
The 5,610-metre volcano in the Alborz is the highest peak in the whole of western Asia, and features on Iranian banknotes.
Which mountain is the highest point of Taiwan?
At 3,952 metres it is higher than anything in Japan or Korea, on an island barely 400 km across.
Which mountain is the highest point of North Korea?
The 2,744-metre volcano on the Chinese border holds a huge crater lake, and the state's founding myth is set on it.
Roughly how high is the highest point of the Maldives?
No country on Earth has a lower summit, which is why a rising sea is an existential question there rather than a forecast.
Which mountain is the highest point of both Uganda and DR Congo?
Its Margherita Peak reaches 5,110 metres in the Rwenzori — the range the ancients called the Mountains of the Moon.
Which mountain is the highest point of Chad?
A 3,445-metre volcano rising straight out of the Sahara in the Tibesti, with a crater some twelve kilometres wide.
Which peak on the Lesotho border is the highest ground in South Africa?
The 3,450-metre peak sits on the Lesotho border in the Drakensberg, and was only settled as the national summit in 1951.
Which mountain is the highest point of Lesotho?
At 3,482 metres it tops all of southern Africa — and the lowest ground in the country is still above 1,400 metres.
Which is the longest river that runs through only one country?
Its 6,300 km lie entirely within China. Every river longer than it crosses at least one border.
Into which sea does the Amur empty?
For much of its 4,444 km the river is the border between Russia and China, which has made it a flashpoint.
Into which sea does the Indus empty?
The river rises in Tibet and gave India its name, yet almost all of its 3,180 km now run through Pakistan.
Which African river empties into the Gulf of Guinea?
Its 4,200 km swing north into the Sahara and back again before the delta in Nigeria — a course that baffled mapmakers for centuries.
Into which gulf does the Colorado river drain?
So much of the 2,945-km river is drawn off for farms and cities that in most years it never reaches the sea at all.
Which river's basin is shared by fifteen countries, more than any other?
Europe's second longest river gathers water from Germany to Ukraine over its 2,888 km.
Which strait separates peninsular Malaysia from Sumatra?
One of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth narrows to under 40 km here, which has made it a pirates' water for centuries.
Which strait separates mainland Australia from Tasmania?
It is shallow enough that during the last ice age it was dry land, and people walked across to Tasmania.
Which strait separates Australia from New Guinea?
Its islands belong to Australia even though some of them lie within sight of the Papuan shore.
Which 70-km strait joins the Adriatic to the Ionian Sea?
Italy and Albania face each other across it, and it has been swum in relay by teams from both shores.
The Kerch Strait leads from the Black Sea into which sea?
The sea it opens into is the shallowest in the world, averaging only about seven metres deep.
Which strait separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea?
Its name means the gate of tears, and it is the Red Sea's only way out to the Indian Ocean.
Which strait does the causeway out of Singapore cross?
The embankment carries a road, a railway and the water pipe Singapore long depended on, over a gap barely a kilometre wide.
Which sea arm separates Jutland from the Swedish province of Halland?
Together with the Skagerrak it is the only sea road between the Baltic and the North Sea.
Which two countries in South America are landlocked?
Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in the 1880s and has never accepted it, keeping a navy on Lake Titicaca to this day.
Which is the largest landlocked country in the world?
It is bigger than all of western Europe put together, and its Caspian shore counts as a lake coast, not a sea one.
Which Asian country is surrounded only by other landlocked countries?
Only one other country is doubly landlocked like this, and it is tiny Liechtenstein in the Alps.
Which is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia?
It is wrapped around the Mekong, which serves as its highway, its border and its power station at once.
Which two continents have no landlocked countries at all?
Every state in both is either an island or keeps its own stretch of coast — Africa alone has sixteen without one.
Which two countries each have fourteen neighbours, more than any others?
Both are vast enough to reach from Europe into Asia, and the two of them of course border each other.
Which two countries are divided by just 155 metres of frontier at Kazungula?
The stub of frontier is at Kazungula, where four African countries come within a few hundred metres of meeting at a point.
How many countries does Canada border?
The United States is the obvious one. The other is Greenland, which meets Canada on the uninhabited Hans Island.
Which country has 39 separate land borders although it has only four neighbours?
Its border with the Netherlands alone breaks into 31 pieces, thanks to the tangle of enclaves at Baarle.
Which is the largest desert in Asia?
Its 2.33 million km² cover most of the Arabian peninsula — nearly twice the Gobi, which usually gets the credit.
Which is the largest desert in southern Africa?
Its 900,000 km² of red sand hold enough grass to graze herds, which is why it is not quite a true desert.
Which is the largest desert in South America?
Its 673,000 km² lie in the rain shadow of the Andes, and are cold and wind-scoured rather than hot.
Which is the largest desert in North America?
Its 492,000 km² sit between the Sierra Nevada and the Rockies, and no drop of its water reaches any sea.
Which is the deepest lake in North America?
It reaches 614 metres in Canada's Northwest Territories — half again as deep as any of the Great Lakes.
Which lake lies buried beneath about four kilometres of Antarctic ice?
Some 900 metres deep and sealed off for millions of years, it was found by radar rather than by eye.
Which deep mountain lake in Kyrgyzstan never freezes over?
It is 668 metres deep and slightly salty, and that salt together with hot springs keeps the ice off all winter.
Which is the highest volcano in the world?
At 6,893 metres on the Argentina–Chile border it is dormant, and holds the world's highest lake near its summit.
Which volcano is the highest peak in Italy south of the Alps?
It stands 3,369 metres over Sicily and is among the most continuously active volcanoes anywhere on Earth.
Which city is the capital of Nigeria?
It was built from nothing in the middle of the country and took over in 1991, because Lagos was too crowded and too Yoruba.
Which city is the capital of Morocco?
Casablanca is far bigger and far better known, but the king and the government sit in the quieter coastal city.
Which city is the capital of Tanzania?
The government began moving inland in 1973 and finished only decades later; several ministries never left the coast.
Which city is the official capital of Ivory Coast?
The president moved it to his home village in 1983 and built a basilica there taller than St Peter's dome.
Which city is the capital of Cameroon?
Douala is the bigger city and the country's port, but the government stays up in the hills inland.
Which city is the official capital of Benin?
Cotonou holds the government, the port and the airport; the official capital keeps little more than the title.
Which city is the administrative capital of Eswatini?
The country has two capitals: this one runs the administration, while the king and parliament sit at Lobamba.
Which city is the capital of Malawi?
It took over from Zomba in 1975, and Blantyre is still the country's commercial centre.
Which city is the capital of Zambia?
Livingstone, by the Victoria Falls, held the title until 1935, when the government moved to the railway junction.
Which city is the capital of Zimbabwe?
It was called Salisbury until 1982, after the British prime minister in office when the city was founded.
Which city is the capital of Mozambique?
It was Lourenço Marques under Portuguese rule, and sits so far south it is closer to Pretoria than to its own north.
Which city is the capital of Angola?
Founded by the Portuguese in 1576, it has repeatedly been ranked the most expensive city in the world for foreign staff.
Which city is the capital of the Republic of the Congo?
It faces Kinshasa across the river — the only place on Earth where two countries' capitals look straight at each other.
Which city is the capital of Gabon?
Its name means free town: it was founded in 1849 for Africans freed from a captured slave ship.
Which city is the capital of Chad?
It was Fort-Lamy until 1973, and stands where the Chari and Logone rivers meet on the Cameroonian border.
Which city is the capital of South Sudan?
It became a capital in 2011, when the country split from Sudan after decades of war.
Which city is the capital of Eritrea?
Its centre is full of 1930s Italian modernist buildings, and is listed as a World Heritage site for them.
Which city is the capital of the Seychelles?
It is one of the smallest capitals in the world, and the whole country has fewer people than a mid-sized Finnish city.
Which city is the capital of Cape Verde?
The name is simply the Portuguese word for beach, and the city sits on the island of Santiago.
Which of South Africa's three capitals is the judicial one?
The courts sit there, the government in Pretoria and parliament in Cape Town — a compromise from the 1910 union.
Which city is Bolivia's constitutional capital?
The constitution names it, but the president and congress have sat in La Paz since a civil war in 1899.
Which city was Brazil's seat of government before Brasília was built?
It held the title from 1763 to 1960, and was even the capital of the whole Portuguese empire for a time.
In which city does Chile's national congress sit?
The government is in Santiago, but the legislature was moved to the port city in 1990 after the dictatorship.
Which city does Peru call its historical capital?
It was the centre of the Inca empire. Lima governs, and Arequipa carries the odd title of legal capital.
Which city is the capital of Guyana?
Much of it lies below high tide and is kept dry by a sea wall and a system of Dutch-built canals.
Which city is the capital of Suriname?
Its wooden Dutch colonial centre is a World Heritage site, and Dutch is still the country's official language.
Which city is the capital of Uganda?
The airport and the old colonial seat are at Entebbe on the lake, some 40 km from the capital itself.
Which Finnish region is the only one with two capitals?
Kotka is the official regional centre and Kouvola the administrative one, a split no other region has.
Which is the smallest Finnish region by area?
Its 1,553 km² of land is less than a sixtieth of Lapland, yet it has its own parliament and its own laws.
Which Finnish region elected its regional council by popular vote from 2004 to 2012?
It was a government experiment in regional self-rule; everywhere else the councils are picked by the municipalities.
Which is the largest national park in Finland?
Its 2,850 km² of Lapland wilderness beat the better-known Urho Kekkonen park by some 300 km².
Which is the smallest national park in Finland?
Just 2.5 km² of land, scattered over islands off the Lapland coast where the land is still rising out of the sea.
Which is Finland's newest national park, established in 2022?
It protects fells and old forest in eastern Lapland, in a municipality better known for its wartime front line.
Which Finnish national park was established in 2017?
It was founded for the centenary of Finnish independence, and holds rock paintings thousands of years old.
Which national park was founded in 2011 alongside Sipoonkorpi?
At 913 km² it is one of Finland's largest parks, and almost all of it is water rather than land.
Above which lake do the cliffs of Koli rise?
The view over its 894 km² from the Koli ridge was painted so often that it became a national landscape.
Into which sea does Lake Inari ultimately drain?
Almost every Finnish lake runs to the Baltic, but this one empties north through the Paatsjoki into the Arctic.
Which Finnish municipality covers more ground than several European countries?
Its 15,060 km² hold fewer than seven thousand people — about one person for every two square kilometres.
Which is the smallest Finnish municipality by land area?
Six square kilometres, entirely surrounded by Espoo, and it has refused to be swallowed by it since 1920.
Enontekiö, Inari, Sodankylä and Utsjoki together make up which special area?
Sámi has official standing there, and the four municipalities cover a corner of Finland bigger than Belgium.
At the present rate of land uplift, Finland and Sweden will join at which strait?
The seabed there is rising about eight millimetres a year, and the gap should close in some two thousand years.
Roughly how much of Finland's land was once under water after the ice age?
Old shorelines are found 150 metres up in the south and over 200 metres up in the east.
Roughly how long is Finland's coastline when every island is counted?
Measured as a smooth line it would be a fraction of that; the archipelago is what makes the number absurd.
Which plain along the Gulf of Bothnia is the largest in the Nordic countries?
The land there is flat because it was sea floor until recently, and it is still rising a few millimetres a year.
At 362 km² it is modest by Nordic standards, and a wooden paddle steamer from 1856 still works on it.
Which is the deepest lake in Europe?
It goes down 514 metres in western Norway, and its floor lies well below sea level.
Counted as one watercourse it runs 720 km, rising in Norway and ending at Gothenburg.
Which is the southernmost point of Sweden?
The low headland near Trelleborg is the southernmost point of the Scandinavian peninsula; Denmark reaches further south still.
Which of Sweden's three historic lands covers nearly 60 per cent of the country?
It holds most of the land and the fewest people, and the provinces inside it stretch from Dalarna to Lapland.
Which is the largest lake in Europe?
Its 17,700 km² lie in Russia, just east of Finland's old border, and it is nearly four times Vänern.
Which lake forms most of the border between Estonia and Russia?
Europe's fifth largest lake freezes hard enough to drive across, which has made the frontier on it awkward to police.

Some 230 km long, it carries meltwater off Vatnajökull and now runs through a chain of power stations.
Which Icelandic island rose out of the sea in an eruption between 1963 and 1967?
It has been left to nature ever since, so that scientists can watch life arrive on brand new ground.
Which Icelandic peninsula was struck by some 17,000 earthquakes in one week in 2021?
The swarm came before an eruption that ended eight centuries of quiet on the peninsula.
Which drained fjord is the lowest point in Denmark, seven metres below sea level?
It was pumped dry in the 1870s for farmland, and the carrots grown in its soil have their own protected name.
How far from the sea is the most inland spot in Denmark?
The country is so cut about by fjords and belts that nowhere in it is much more than an hour's drive from salt water.
Which Nordic cross flag is the oldest, dating from the 13th century?
The Dannebrog's white cross on red goes back to the first half of the 13th century; the others copied it later.
Which Nordic country's flag was the first to use three colours?
A blue cross was set inside the white one on red, so that the flag carried the colours of both Denmark and Sweden.
Which is the highest capital city in the world?
At 3,640 metres the air holds about a third less oxygen than at sea level, so arriving visitors are routinely laid out by it.
Which national capital lies furthest below sea level?
It sits 28 metres down on the shore of the Caspian, which is itself the lowest large body of water on Earth.
Which is the highest capital city in Europe?
At 1,023 metres in the Pyrenees it is more than 350 metres above Madrid, which is Europe's highest big-country capital.
Which is the highest capital city in Asia?
The Bhutanese capital sits at 2,334 metres — nearly a kilometre higher than Kathmandu, which most people would pick.
Which capital city lies about two metres below sea level?
The city is held dry by dikes and pumps, and its name records the dam built across the Amstel to start the job.
Which is the highest capital city in Africa?
At 2,355 metres it is cool enough all year that the city barely needs the word summer, though it sits near the equator.
Which Belgian town is split into 22 separate parcels inside the Netherlands?
Some houses have the border through them, and the front door decides which country you are in — so doors have been moved.
Which Spanish town is an enclave entirely inside France?
A treaty in 1659 handed France the surrounding villages but not this one, because it was legally a town and not a village.
Which German village is completely surrounded by Switzerland?
It is German territory inside the Swiss customs area, so it uses Swiss francs and has two postcodes and two phone codes.
Which Italian town lies entirely within Switzerland?
It sits on Lake Lugano, kept by Italy since the Middle Ages, and for decades its casino was its whole economy.
Which Austrian village can only be reached by road through Germany?
It hangs off Austria by a single mountain summit, where the two countries touch at one point and nowhere else.
Which country's exclave of Madha contains a village belonging to another state?
Inside Madha sits Nahwa, which belongs to the UAE — an enclave within an exclave, settled by local rulers' choice in the 1930s.
Which country owns Likoma Island, although it lies in Mozambique's waters?
Missionaries built a cathedral there in the 1900s, and the island stayed British — and then Malawian — because of the church.
Which country has the most time zones?
Twelve of them, almost none in Europe: the count comes from territories scattered across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans.
Which country is wide enough for five time zones but keeps a single clock?
Everything runs on Beijing time, so in the far west the sun can rise at ten in the morning and an unofficial local time is used.
Which country's clocks run 45 minutes off the hour?
It sits at UTC+05:45, a quarter-hour away from India, which the Nepalese chose deliberately as a mark of independence.
Which Pacific island country spans three time zones, from UTC+12 to UTC+14?
Its eastern islands are two hours ahead of its western ones, and it moved the date line in 1995 so the whole country shared a day.
Which Canadian island province keeps its clocks half an hour off its neighbours?
It runs at UTC−03:30, a half-hour offset kept since the days when the island set its time by the sun over St John's.
Which is the second largest island in Europe?
At 101,826 km² it beats Ireland by some 17,000 km² — and holds about a twentieth of Ireland's people.
Which is the largest island in Canada?
Its 507,000 km² make it larger than Sweden, and fewer than fifteen thousand people live on the whole of it.
Which of New Zealand's two main islands is the larger?
The South Island is some 36,000 km² bigger, yet three in four New Zealanders live on the smaller one.
Which island is divided between Argentina and Chile?
The two countries came close to war over the channels around it in 1978, and the Pope was asked to arbitrate.
Which city is the official capital of Sri Lanka?
Parliament and the courts were moved out to a suburb in the 1980s; Colombo kept the port, the business and the fame.
Which city is the capital of Myanmar?
The generals built it inland and moved the government there in 2005, into streets so wide and empty they are famous for it.
Which city is the capital of Belize?
A hurricane flattened Belize City in 1961, so a new capital was laid out fifty miles inland, out of the storm's reach.
Enclaves on both sides give which two countries six separate borders?
Each holds scraps of land inside the other, left behind when Soviet republics were drawn up and never tidied away.
Which is the second largest desert on Earth?
A desert is measured by how little rain falls, not by heat, so both polar regions outrank the Sahara.
Which country shares Mont Blanc, its own highest point, with France?
The summit's ownership has never been fully agreed, and Italian and French maps have drawn the border differently for two centuries.
Who wrote Hytti nro 6, the Finlandia Prize winner of 2011?
The novel follows a train journey across the Soviet Union and was later filmed.
Who won the very first Finlandia Prize, in 1984?
His Yksinäisyys ja uhma opened a prize that has shaped Finnish book autumns ever since.
Which novel won Bo Carpelan the Finlandia Prize in 1993?
Carpelan wrote in Swedish and is one of the few to have taken the prize twice.
A man who loses his family and sets out to win back a house in the right postcode.
Who brought trolls into modern Helsinki in Ennen päivänlaskua ei voi?
The novel put trolls into modern Helsinki and is counted as Finnish weird fiction.
Which novel won Olli Jalonen the Finlandia Prize in 2018?
Jalonen had already won in 1990, making him one of the prize's repeat winners.
Who wrote Oneiron, set in the seconds after death?
Oneiron takes place in the seconds after death, with seven women in a white void.
In which year was the Finlandia Prize awarded for the first time?
Since 1993 the fiction prize has gone to novels only, and publishers alone may enter books.
Who chooses the Finlandia Prize winner from the shortlist?
A single chooser named for that year
The board of the Finnish Writers' Union
The chooser is announced in advance, and the choice is theirs alone to defend.
Who may enter a book for the Finlandia Prize?
The Finnish Book Foundation runs the prize and says it is there to celebrate reading.
Who wrote Is, a novel of the Åland skerries just after the war?
Is is set in the Åland skerries just after the war and was written in Swedish.

Thulium was the last of the Ytterby earths to be teased apart, and its name points at the half-legendary edge of the known world.
The element holmium takes its name from the Latin name of which capital city?
Holmia is Latin for Stockholm. Its neighbour hafnium comes from Hafnia, which is Copenhagen, so two capitals sit side by side on the table.
Vanadium is named after Vanadis, another name for which Norse goddess?
The Swedish chemist chose Freyja's byname because vanadium's compounds come in such startling colours, from green to violet.
The name of which metal comes from the Swedish word kopparnickel?
Kopparnickel meant a copper-coloured ore that stubbornly gave no copper, so the miners blamed a trickster spirit, Old Nick.
Which element's name comes from a German word for a goblin that miners blamed for bad ore?
A Kobold was the spirit held responsible when an ore poisoned the smelters and yielded no metal; cobalt ore carries arsenic.
Selenium is named from the Greek word for which heavenly body?
Selene was the moon goddess. The element next to it on the table, tellurium, is named from tellus, the Earth, so the pair are moon and earth.
Which element's name comes from the Latin word for the Earth?
Tellus is Latin for the Earth. It was named by the man who found it in gold ore from Transylvania.
Which gas takes its name from a Greek word meaning simply 'new'?
Neos means new; krypton beside it means hidden and xenon means stranger. The whole shelf was named for how hard it was to find.
Argon's name is Greek for which quality?
It refused to react with anything the chemists offered it, so they called it the lazy one. That inertness is why welders shelter hot steel in it.
Bromine's name comes from a Greek word for what?
Bromos means a stink, and bromine earns it. Osmium is named the same way, after the reek of its oxide.
Chlorine is named after which property of the gas?
Chloros is Greek for yellowish green. Chromium was named the same way, from chroma, because its compounds are so many-coloured.
Heated iodine gives off a vapour of which colour, the colour its name means?
The solid is almost black, but heat it and the vapour is a deep violet. That vapour is what the namer saw.
Phosphorus is named from Greek roots meaning what?
White phosphorus glows faintly in air of its own accord, and the word phosphorescence comes from the same root.
Osmium's name comes from the Greek for which thing?
Osmium tetroxide reeks and attacks the eyes, so the densest metal known was named for its stink rather than its weight.
Iridium is named from the Latin word iris, meaning what?
Its salts come in many strong colours. A thin layer of iridium in the rock is also the fingerprint of the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
Tantalum is named after Tantalus, and niobium after which relative of his?
The two metals occur together and are maddeningly hard to separate, so the chemist gave them names from the same family.
Platinum's name comes from a Spanish word meaning what?
Spanish miners met it in silver workings, could not melt it, and dismissed it as platina, a lesser silver.
Filament bulbs used a metal whose symbol is W. Which metal?
W stands for wolfram, the old German name, while the English name came from Swedish tung sten, heavy stone. It has the highest melting point of any metal.
The symbol Sb belongs to which element?
Sb is from stibium, the Latin name of the black eye paint ground from antimony ore and worn in ancient Egypt.
The symbol Cu comes from cuprum, a word the Romans took from which island?
Cyprus was the empire's copper mine, and aes cyprium, metal of Cyprus, wore down to cuprum and then to copper.
The symbol Pb for lead comes from plumbum, which also gave English which word?
Roman water pipes were lead, so the man who worked them was a plumbarius, and the trade still carries the metal's name.
How many elements does the periodic table name today?
It runs from hydrogen at 1 to oganesson at 118. Everything heavier than uranium at 92 has to be built in a laboratory, an atom at a time.
The oxygen family, group 16 of the periodic table, goes by which name?
Oxygen, sulfur, selenium and tellurium. The name means ore formers, because so many metal ores are oxides or sulfides.
Nitrogen and phosphorus head group 15, known as what?
The name comes from a Greek root for choking: nitrogen smothers a flame, and that is how it was first noticed.
Copper, silver and gold together are traditionally called what?
Group 11 has been struck into money for three thousand years because it resists corrosion but is still soft enough to stamp.
Which of these sits in the same periodic group as carbon?
Group 14. Silicon lies straight below carbon and can also build long chains, which is why science fiction keeps inventing silicon life.
Which element shares group 1 with the alkali metals despite being a gas?
Hydrogen has one outer electron, like lithium and sodium, so the table puts it at the head of the column even though it behaves nothing like a metal.
Which gas is the third most common in the air we breathe?
Argon makes up almost one per cent of the atmosphere, twenty-five times more than carbon dioxide, and does absolutely nothing while it is there.
Electric charge is measured in which unit?
One coulomb is the charge one ampere carries past a point in a second. A lightning bolt moves perhaps fifteen of them.
Capacitance is measured in which unit?
A one-farad capacitor would be enormous, so the ones in a phone are measured in millionths of a farad.
It is a coil's resistance to a change of current, and it is why a fluorescent tube needs a heavy ballast.
Magnetic flux density is measured in which unit?
A hospital scanner runs at one to three tesla. The Earth's own field, which swings a compass, is about fifty millionths of one.
Electrical conductance is measured in which unit?
The siemens is resistance turned upside down: one siemens is one reciprocal ohm, and it used to be called the mho.
Radioactivity itself is measured in which unit?
One becquerel is a single atom decaying each second, so a human body, which is mildly radioactive, runs at several thousand.
The dose of radiation a person receives is given in which unit?
It is named after the Swede Rolf Sievert, who worked out how to measure what a dose actually does to tissue.
Which unit counts the energy that ionising radiation dumps into each kilogram?
The gray measures the raw energy absorbed; the sievert then weights it by how much harm that kind of radiation does.
The light actually falling on a surface is measured in which unit?
An overcast day gives a thousand lux outdoors and a desk needs five hundred, which is why offices feel dim next to the street.
The total light a lamp gives out is measured in which unit?
Bulbs are now sold in lumens rather than watts, because watts only said how much electricity went in, not how much light came out.
Which SI base unit measures luminous intensity?
Candela is Latin for candle, and the unit was originally pinned to the light of one standard candle.
A solid angle is measured in which unit?
A whole sphere holds four pi steradians, which is exactly why brightness falls off as the square of the distance.
The ångström, a ten-billionth of a metre, honours a scientist from which country?
Anders Ångström of Uppsala helped found spectroscopy. Atoms are a few ångströms across, which is why the unit survives in chemistry.
The svedberg unit describes how fast something does what?
Theodor Svedberg won a Nobel for spinning things apart, and ribosomes are still named by their svedberg value, as in 70S.
Roughly how many particles are there in one mole?
The Avogadro number is now fixed by definition at 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third, so the mole no longer depends on a lump of carbon.
Which constant gives the charge carried by a single electron?
It is 1.602 times ten to the minus nineteenth coulombs, and since 2019 this number is what defines the ampere.
Roughly what is the molar gas constant used in the ideal gas law?
About 8.3 joules per mole per kelvin
About 83 joules per mole per kelvin
About 0.83 joules per mole per kelvin
About 830 joules per mole per kelvin
8.314 ties pressure, volume and temperature together for any well-behaved gas, and it is just the Boltzmann constant times the Avogadro number.
A proton is heavier than an electron by roughly what factor?
The proton weighs 1.673 times ten to the minus twenty-seventh kilograms. Nearly all an atom's mass sits in that tiny nucleus.

He showed that cathode rays are a stream of particles nearly two thousand times lighter than the lightest atom.
The nucleus had been too heavy for its charge for twenty years. The missing neutral particle explained it, and made the atom bomb thinkable.
Who worked out in 1911 that an atom is mostly empty space around a tiny nucleus?
He fired alpha particles at gold foil. Almost all went straight through, but one in eight thousand bounced back, which he said was like a shell rebounding off tissue paper.
He cooled mercury with liquid helium to four degrees above absolute zero and watched its electrical resistance vanish entirely.
Move a magnet through a coil and a current appears. Every power station in the world still earns its living on that one observation.
Who noticed in 1820 that an electric current swings a compass needle?
The Dane spotted it during a lecture. It was the first evidence that electricity and magnetism are one thing, and a unit of magnetism carries his name.
Which Danish scientist first produced metallic aluminium, in 1824?
His sample was impure and nobody noticed. Aluminium stayed more precious than silver for another sixty years.
Which Swedish apothecary discovered chlorine, manganese, molybdenum and tungsten?
He also found oxygen on his own, but Priestley published first, so Scheele is remembered as chemistry's unluckiest man.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele called the gas he had discovered by which name?
The gas was oxygen. Scheele tasted and sniffed everything he made, including hydrogen cyanide, and was dead at 43.
Which Danish seismologist showed in 1936 that the Earth has a solid inner core?
She read it off wave arrivals that should not have existed, from a New Zealand earthquake recorded in Siberia. She lived to 104.
Who introduced the pH scale, in 1909?
The p stood for the German Wasserstoffionenexponent, hydrogen ion exponent, which is why nobody can agree what the p means now.
In which Copenhagen laboratory was the pH scale devised?
A brewery laboratory. Beer lives and dies by acidity, and the Carlsberg founder had endowed it to do real science.
Which Danish astronomer first showed that light travels at a finite speed?
In 1676 he timed eclipses of a moon of Jupiter and found them running eleven minutes late when the Earth was on the far side of its orbit.
Which of Jupiter's moons did Ole Rømer time to catch light out?
Io is the innermost of the four big moons and swings behind Jupiter every forty-two hours, so he had a clock that ticked often.
Dynamite is nitroglycerin soaked into which absorbent material?
Kieselguhr is the chalky rock of fossil algae. Soaked in it, a liquid that exploded if you looked at it became safe to carry up a mountain.
How many prize categories did Alfred Nobel's will set up?
Physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The economics prize is not his: a bank added it in 1968 and paid for the name.
Which Finn won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on cattle feed?
His method let a farm keep summer grass through a Finnish winter, which in the 1930s mattered more than almost any laboratory result.
What did A. I. Virtanen add to green fodder to keep it through the winter?
Dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid stopped the fermentation that destroys the nutrients, without harming the cattle that ate it.
What is Carl Linnaeus's great classifying work called?
First printed in 1735 as eleven large pages, it had swollen to three thousand by its twelfth edition.
Who first described and named the cell, in 1665?
Looking at a slice of cork, he thought the empty boxes looked like the bare rooms monks slept in, and called them cells.
Who first saw living microorganisms through a microscope, in 1675?
A Delft draper with no scientific training ground better lenses than anyone in Europe and called what swam under them his little animals.
Who worked out how blood circulates round the body, in 1628?
He proved the heart pumps the same blood round and round, by showing it moves far too much of it for the liver to be making it fresh.
Who made the first polio vaccine, in 1952?
He refused to patent it. Asked who owned it, he said you might as well patent the Sun.
Who isolated insulin in 1922 and turned it into a treatment?
Children who had been dying in diabetic coma in a Toronto ward woke up as the injections went round the room.
Who took Photo 51, the X-ray image that revealed DNA's shape?
She and Raymond Gosling made it in 1952. She died of cancer at 37 in 1958, and the Nobel is never awarded after death.
Which technique produced the picture that showed DNA to be a helix?
Fire X-rays through a crystal and the scattered beams make a pattern of spots. Read the spots and the shape of the molecule falls out.
Who shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for the structure of DNA with Watson and Crick?
Wilkins had shown Watson his colleague Franklin's X-ray image, without telling her, and that was the moment the helix became obvious.
Who discovered the four main human blood groups, around 1900?
Before his work a transfusion was a coin toss, because mismatched blood clumps in the vein and kills within minutes.
Who split the uranium nucleus in 1938, discovering nuclear fission?
Lise Meitner worked out what the chemistry meant from exile in Sweden. The Nobel went to Hahn alone.
Which work won Albert Einstein his Nobel Prize in Physics?
The equivalence of mass and energy
Relativity was thought too speculative in 1921, so the prize went to his 1905 paper proposing that light comes in packets.
Which Swede won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the theory of ions in solution?
His examiners had nearly failed the same idea as a doctoral thesis twenty years earlier.
Which Swede won a Nobel Prize in 2022 for reading the genomes of extinct humans?
His group sequenced Neanderthal DNA from old bone and showed that a few per cent of it survives in people alive today.
Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
Ganymede is 2,634 km in radius, wider than the planet Mercury, and it is the only moon known to have a magnetic field of its own.
Which large moon orbits its planet backwards?
Triton circles Neptune the wrong way, which means it was almost certainly captured rather than formed there, and it is slowly spiralling in.
Which two planets have no moons at all?
Both sit too close to the Sun to hold on to a satellite. Mars, further out, manages two small captured lumps.
Mars's two moons, Phobos and Deimos, are named after which pair of ideas?
They were the attendants of Ares, the god of war, so the war planet keeps fear and dread in orbit around it.
Which of these is not one of Jupiter's four Galilean moons?
Galileo saw four moons through his telescope in 1610, and the sight ended the idea that everything circles the Earth. Triton belongs to Neptune.
Which is the largest moon of Uranus?
Titania is 1,577 km across, and William Herschel found it and Oberon in 1787, six years after he found the planet itself.
The moons of Uranus are named after characters from whose works?
Titania, Oberon and Miranda come from Shakespeare; Ariel and Umbriel from Alexander Pope's poem The Rape of the Lock.
Which moon of Uranus is named after a gnome in a poem by Alexander Pope?
Umbriel was the melancholy gnome of The Rape of the Lock, and the moon is the darkest of the five big Uranian satellites.
Which planet has the longest day?
One turn on its axis takes Venus about 243 Earth days, which is longer than its year of 225 days.
Which planet turns on its axis fastest?
Jupiter gets round in under ten hours despite being the biggest planet, and the spin flattens it visibly at the poles.
On which planet would the Sun rise in the west?
Venus spins backwards, so the Sun there would rise in the west, and very slowly at that.
Where does the Earth come when the eight planets are ranked by size?
The four giants come first, then Earth, then Venus, Mars and Mercury. Earth is the biggest of the rocky four.
Which is the widest of the four rocky planets?
Earth beats Venus by about 650 km, which is a whisker. Among the giants the margin is just as fine: Uranus is wider than Neptune but lighter.
Roughly how many times further from the Sun is Neptune than the Earth?
Neptune sits 30 astronomical units out, so sunlight there is a thousandth as strong and noon looks like deep twilight.
Which layer of the atmosphere lies directly above the stratosphere?
The mesosphere runs from about 50 to 85 km up. It is the coldest part of the atmosphere, and where most meteors burn out.
The ionosphere sits inside which layer of the atmosphere?
The thermosphere reaches past 600 km, and its charged gas both bounces radio waves round the world and lights up as the aurora.
Which is the outermost layer of the Earth's atmosphere?
It begins somewhere above 500 km and thins out to about 10,000 km, where the last stray atoms give up and drift into space.
In a cloud's Latin name, what does the word nimbus tell you?
It is a sign of fair weather
Nimbostratus and cumulonimbus both carry it. Luke Howard built the scheme in 1802 so that a cloud's name would describe what it was about to do.
In cloud names, which prefix marks the highest clouds?
Cirrus clouds float above six kilometres and are made of ice crystals, which is why they look like drawn-out white hair.
Which clouds form highest of all, in the mesosphere about 80 km up?
They glow silvery-blue in a dark summer sky, lit by sunlight that no longer reaches the ground, and northern Europe sees them best.
Who devised the Latin naming scheme for clouds, in 1802?
He was a London chemist who watched clouds as a hobby, and his names were so good that meteorology still uses them unchanged.
Which cloud genus is the thin, wispy, almost transparent one made of ice?
Cirrus means a curl of hair in Latin. A sky filling with it often means a warm front and rain within a day.
Marble is limestone that has been changed by heat and pressure. What kind of rock does that make it?
Squeeze and bake a limestone and its shelly grains recrystallise into the even sugary texture a sculptor wants.
Quartzite started out as which rock?
Heat welds a sandstone's grains together until the rock breaks through the grains rather than between them.
Slate is formed from which rock?
The clay flakes in shale line up under pressure, which is why slate splits into the flat sheets that roof a house.
Which of these is a sedimentary rock made from dead plants?
Peat buried deep enough loses its water and turns to coal, so a seam of coal is a compressed swamp.
Which volcanic rock is a natural glass that was knapped into blades?
Lava cooled too fast for crystals to grow, so it froze as glass. A fresh obsidian edge is sharper than a surgical scalpel.
Which igneous rock is light enough to float on water?
Froth thrown out of a volcano sets with so much trapped gas that rafts of it drift across oceans after an eruption.
Which of these is a metamorphic rock?
Gneiss is granite cooked and squeezed until it shows bands. Much of the Finnish bedrock is gneiss nearly two thousand million years old.
Chalk belongs to which of the three great rock groups?
Chalk is the shells of countless microscopic sea creatures, laid down grain by grain on an ancient sea floor.
What is a metamorphic rock called when heat and pressure have given it visible banding?
Slate, schist and gneiss are all foliated; marble and quartzite are not, which is why marble takes a polish so evenly.
Granite cooled slowly deep underground. Where did basalt cool?
Basalt is lava that chilled in the open, so its crystals never had time to grow and the rock looks almost featureless dark grey.
Which of these dinosaurs lived in the Late Triassic?
Plateosaurus was one of the first really large plant-eaters, walking Europe when dinosaurs were still a new idea.
Which long-necked giant stretched 25 metres across the Late Jurassic?
Diplodocus stretched 25 metres, most of it neck and tail. Triceratops and Velociraptor came tens of millions of years later.
Which of the three dinosaur periods came first?
Triassic, then Jurassic, then Cretaceous. The first dinosaurs appear about 237 million years ago, well into the Triassic.
Which feathered Late Jurassic animal sits in the museum's dinosaur directory?
Archaeopteryx had feathers and a wishbone but also teeth and a long bony tail, and it settled the argument about where birds came from.
Which of these was an early dinosaur barely a metre long?
Eoraptor was about a metre long and ran on two legs. The giants came much later; everything started small.
An adult rib cage holds how many ribs?
Twelve pairs, and the bottom two pairs are floating ribs, joined to the spine but not to the breastbone.
How many vertebrae are there in the thoracic part of the spine?
One for each pair of ribs. The neck has seven and the lower back five, which is why the chest is the stiffest part of the spine.
How many vertebrae make up the lower back?
Five lumbar vertebrae carry the whole weight of the upper body, which is why they are the biggest and the ones that give out.
The sacrum at the base of the spine is formed from how many fused vertebrae?
Five grow together into one solid plate that wedges into the pelvis and takes the load from the spine into the legs.
Which bone is the last remnant of a tail?
Three to five vertebrae fused into a stub. It still anchors muscles of the pelvic floor, so it is not quite useless.
How many bones are there in one human hand and wrist?
Eight in the wrist, five in the palm and fourteen in the fingers. Both hands together hold more than a quarter of all your bones.
One human foot contains how many bones?
Seven in the ankle, five in the arch and fourteen in the toes. One foot therefore has one fewer bone than one hand.
How many bones make up the human skull?
Eight in the braincase and fourteen in the face. They are separate plates in a baby, which is what lets the head squeeze through at birth.
What is the medical name for the heel bone?
It is the biggest bone in the foot, and the Achilles tendon fastens to the back of it.
Which two bones make up the human forearm?
They cross over each other, and that is the trick that lets you turn your palm up and down.
Which is the thinner of the two bones in the lower leg?
The tibia carries the weight; the slender fibula on the outside mostly anchors muscle and steadies the ankle.
What are the three small bones of the middle ear called as a group?
Malleus, incus and stapes: hammer, anvil and stirrup. They are the only bones that never grow after birth.
The spleen belongs to which system of the body?
It filters blood and stores white cells, which is why a person can live without one but catches infections more easily.
Which of these is part of the lymphatic system?
The thymus sits behind the breastbone and schools the body's T cells. It shrinks away almost entirely by middle age.
The pituitary gland belongs to which system?
A pea-sized gland under the brain that commands the thyroid, the adrenals and growth itself. It is the body's control room for hormones.
Which of these is one of the three pairs of salivary glands?
Parotid, submandibular and sublingual. The parotid pair in front of the ears are the ones that swell up in mumps.
Which part of the eye does most of the focusing?
The clear dome at the front bends the light hardest. The lens only fine-tunes it, which is why laser surgery reshapes the cornea.
Which cells in the retina detect colour?
Three kinds of cone between them cover the whole visible spectrum. They need good light, which is why colour drains away at dusk.
Which retinal cells let you see in near darkness?
Rods are far more sensitive but colour-blind, and there are none in the very centre of the retina, so faint stars vanish if you look straight at them.
What is the tough white outer coat of the eye called?
It holds the eyeball's shape under pressure, like the casing of a ball, and the cornea is the clear window set into the front of it.
What fills the inside of the eyeball?
A clear gel that keeps the eye round and holds the retina against the back wall. The floaters you see drifting are specks inside it.
What are the English names of the three middle ear bones?
Malleus, incus and stapes in Latin. Each is named for the blacksmith's tool it looks like under a microscope.
Which tube keeps the pressure inside the middle ear equal to the outside?
It drains into the back of the nose, which is why swallowing clears your ears on a descending aeroplane.
Which structures of the inner ear look after your balance?
Three fluid-filled loops at right angles to each other. Spin round and the fluid keeps moving after you stop, which is dizziness.
What is the proper name for the visible flap of the ear?
Skin over cartilage, shaped to funnel sound inwards and to tell your brain whether a noise came from in front or behind.
Which part of the ear separates the outer ear from the middle ear?
A membrane thinner than paper and about a centimetre across. It moves less than the width of an atom for the quietest sound you can hear.
A shortage of which vitamin causes beriberi?
Thiamine. The disease spread when milling began stripping the husk off rice, because the husk was where the vitamin was.
Pellagra is caused by a shortage of which vitamin?
Niacin. Its course was once summed up as the four Ds: diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia and death.
Night blindness is the first sign of a shortage of which vitamin?
Untreated it goes on to soften the cornea and blind the eye for good, and it is still a leading cause of childhood blindness.
Pernicious anaemia comes from a shortage of which vitamin?
B12 comes almost entirely from animal foods, and absorbing it needs a protein from the stomach, so the illness can strike a good diet.
Which vitamin does the blood need in order to clot?
Newborn babies are short of it, which is why they are given a dose at birth. The K comes from the German Koagulation.
Which vitamin must be plentiful in early pregnancy to close the neural tube?
Folate, or vitamin B9. The damage happens in the first weeks, often before a pregnancy is even known about.
Which four vitamins are the fat-soluble ones?
Because the body stores them in fat, you can take too much of these, while the water-soluble ones simply wash out.
Which blood type can receive a transfusion from any other?
Its plasma carries no anti-A or anti-B antibodies and it has the Rh antigen too, so nothing in donated blood looks foreign to it.
Which antigen decides whether blood is called Rh positive or Rh negative?
The Rh system has many antigens, but D is the one that matters in practice, in transfusions and in pregnancy.
Which antibodies does the plasma of blood group O carry?
Its red cells carry no A or B antigen, so it can be given to anyone, but its plasma will attack almost anyone else's cells.
Which is the largest fish in the sea?
Females average about 14 metres, and the longest reported was 21. For all that size it strains plankton through its gills.
Which is the largest reptile alive today?
Males reach seven metres and a tonne. It swims far out to sea, which is how it reached so many scattered islands.
Roughly how heavy can a blue whale get?
It is the heaviest animal that has ever lived, heavier than the largest dinosaur, and it needs water to hold that weight up.
A blue whale's heart is about the size of what?
Everything scales up: the tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant, and the animal eats four tonnes of krill in a day.
How far does a blue whale's call carry in good conditions?
A thousand miles. They are among the loudest animals alive, and the low notes travel because the deep ocean bends sound back.
Which bird makes the longest migration of any animal?
About 80,000 km on the round trip, from above the Arctic Circle to the Antarctic and back, chasing summer at both ends of the planet.
What do reindeer live on through the winter?
They dig through the snow with a hoof whose underside is hollowed like a scoop, and lichen is almost the only thing left to find.
Why is the underside of a reindeer's hoof hollowed out?
It works as a scoop in winter and as a snowshoe the rest of the year, and its sharp rim grips rock and ice.
Roughly how long has the Saimaa seal been cut off from the sea?
Its ancestors were trapped when the land rose after the last ice age, and the population has been on its own ever since.
What cut the Saimaa seal off from the sea in the first place?
The land rose after the ice age
Freed of the weight of the ice sheet, the ground is still rising today, and it closed the lake behind the seals.
Finland has how many native snakes?
The adder, the grass snake and the smooth snake. Only the adder is venomous, and the smooth snake is so rare most Finns never see one.
The slow worm, found in southern Finland, is actually what?
Anguis fragilis has eyelids and can shed its tail, which snakes cannot do, and it is harmless.
Pine, spruce and birch together make up what share of the trees in Finland's forests?
Almost everything else is a rounding error. Half of Finland's forest is pine forest alone.
Roughly how many tree species grow in Finland?
A short list, because the ice wiped the slate clean and only the hardiest species have walked back north since.
Half of Finland's forest is which kind of forest?
Pine takes the poor, dry and rocky ground that spruce will not have, and most of Finland is exactly that.
What is being built at Onkalo on the island of Olkiluoto?
A final repository for spent nuclear fuel
The spent fuel goes into copper canisters packed in clay, deep in bedrock that has not moved in a very long time.
Roughly how deep into the bedrock does Onkalo go?
Four hundred to four hundred and thirty metres down into crystalline rock, below any groundwater that moves quickly.
The canisters buried at Onkalo are made mostly of which metal?
Copper over a cast iron insert. In oxygen-free rock copper corrodes extraordinarily slowly, which is the whole idea.
What is packed around the canisters in Onkalo's tunnels?
Bentonite swells when it gets wet, so it seals the gap and holds the canister still if the rock ever shifts.
The wolverine belongs to which family of mammals?
It is the biggest land member of the mustelids, and its jaws are built to crack frozen bone that nothing else can use.
Which bird of prey is the only living species in its whole family?
The osprey is found on every continent except Antarctica, lives almost entirely on fish, and has no close relatives at all.
The word raptor comes from a Latin verb meaning what?
Rapio, to seize or take by force, which describes the feet rather than the beak. A raptor kills with its talons.
Eagles, hawks, buzzards, harriers and kites all belong to which family?
Falcons are in a separate family and are not close relatives at all, despite looking the part.
Which long-legged African bird of prey hunts on foot in the grass?
It stalks across the savannah on stilted legs and stamps snakes to death, and it is the only species in its family.
Owls are placed in which order of birds?
A separate order from the daytime raptors. Their resemblance is the result of the same job, not of shared ancestry.
Who picked up the strange black stone at Ytterby in 1787 that started it all?
Carl Axel Arrhenius was an artillery officer and amateur mineralogist. Nine elements were eventually traced to the rock he pocketed.
Johan Gadolin was professor of chemistry at which university?
He held the chair at the Royal Academy of Turku from 1797 to 1822, back when Finland was still part of Sweden.
Which element found at Ytterby is named after a king punished with eternal thirst?
Tantalus stood knee-deep in water he could never drink, which is how the chemist felt trying to dissolve the metal.
Ørsted was the first to extract which pungent compound, from black pepper?

Japan took Taiwan from China in the settlement and held it for the next fifty years.
Which war did the Treaty of Vereeniging end in 1902?
Two Boer republics gave up their independence to Britain after two and a half years of fighting.
Which war did the Treaty of Paris of 1898 end?
Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and with them the last of its empire.
Which war did the Treaty of Knäred end in 1613?
It closed a short war in which Denmark and Sweden fought over control of the far north.
Which treaty of 1832 fixed the borders of the new Greek state?
The Greece it created was far smaller than today's, reaching only a little way north of Athens.
Which war did the Treaty of Addis Ababa end in 1896?
Italy had to recognise Ethiopia as independent, the one clear African victory over a European invader.
Which war did the Treaty of Copenhagen end in 1660?
Denmark got Bornholm back and Norway got Trondheim, and that border has barely moved since.
Which war did the second Treaty of Paris end in 1783?
Britain recognised American independence about two years after the fighting had effectively ended at Yorktown.
Which city was England's capital from 927 to 1066?
It had been the seat of the kings of Wessex, and London only took over after the Norman conquest.
Which city was Italy's first capital after unification in 1861?
Florence took over in 1865, and Rome only in 1871, once the pope's own state had been swallowed.
Which city was the capital of British India until 1911?
The British then moved the capital to Delhi, where an entire new city was laid out for it.
Which city was Pakistan's first capital, from 1947 to 1959?
Rawalpindi then served as a stopgap capital for years while Islamabad was being built from nothing.
Which city was Australia's seat of government until 1927?
Sydney and Melbourne could not agree which should be capital, so a new city was built between them.
Which city was Japan's capital from 794 to 1868?
Nara had held the title before it, and Tokyo only took over when the emperor moved east in 1868.
Which city was West Germany's capital from 1949 to 1990?
A small university town was picked partly because few expected the division of Germany to last.
Which city was the seat of Russia's rulers from 1169 to 1327?
Moscow took the role in 1327 and has held it ever since, apart from two centuries on the Baltic.
Which city was the Ottoman capital from 1365 until 1453?
Bursa had been the first Ottoman capital, and Constantinople became the third after it was taken.
Which city was Poland's royal capital for five centuries from 1296?
Warsaw took over informally from 1596 and formally in 1795; Gniezno had been the first capital of all.
Which city served as Hungary's capital while the Turks held Buda?
Pozsony is today Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia, and it held the role for nearly 250 years.
Which city was the capital of Greece before Athens?
It served the new Greek state from 1821 until the court moved to Athens in 1836.
Finland's warning signs are yellow where most of Europe uses white. Why?
White was already used for speed limits
A white triangle on a white verge is nearly invisible, so Finland and Sweden kept the older yellow.
How many different hoofed animals get a warning sign of their own in Finland?
Four, the fourth being wild boar
Most countries manage with a single deer triangle; Finland is one of the few that separates them.
In the Finnish system, what does a round blue sign tell you?
Shape and colour carry the grammar: round blue commands, round yellow with a red rim forbids, yellow triangle warns.
Which part of Finland has road signs in the Swedish style, lettered only in Swedish?
Åland runs its own road law, so a mainland driver crossing by ferry meets a different alphabet of shapes.
Finland has a warning triangle for a crossroads where nobody has priority. What does it warn of?
That you must give way to the right
That the lights are out of order
That traffic from the left has priority
Most countries leave the give-way-to-the-right rule for the driver to notice; Finland signposts it.
What word is lettered on a Finnish stop sign?
The word stays English across Europe by treaty, so a driver who reads no local language still obeys it.
Two Finnish prohibition signs are blue instead of yellow. Which?
No entry and no through road
Parking rules were given their own colour so that the eye sorts them from the dangers without reading them.
A Finnish roadside sign carrying a figure in megahertz points you to what?
Before a phone could read you the traffic news, the sign was how you found the local broadcast.
At which of Finland's borders is there a sign forbidding you to pass without stopping?
The Russian, Swedish and Norwegian ones
Only the Russian and Norwegian ones
Estonia is the trap: the sea lies between, and Finland has no land border with it at all.
Which of these Finnish signs is a blue order rather than a prohibition?
A minimum limit orders you to keep moving, so it joins the blue family with motorway and one-way signs.
Roughly how long was the Finnish peninkulma before the metric system?
A still older peninkulma of the 1600s was only about six kilometres, so the word nearly doubled in length.
What does the old Finnish counting unit tiu count?
Each trade had its own number: a toltti was twelve planks, a kiihtelys forty pelts, a kerpo thirty-one lampreys.
How many eggs make a tiu?
Twenty was the old shopkeeper's bundle: a puntti of matchboxes counted twenty as well.
What did a Finnish kiihtelys of forty consist of?
Fur was counted and never weighed, and the pelt bundle gave eastern Finland a unit of trade all its own.
The Finnish poronkusema measured roughly what distance?
It was how far a reindeer could pull before it had to stop, and it survives only as a word for very far off.
How far is a kivenheitto in the old Finnish measures?
It was fixed at a hundred kyynärä — a stone's throw turns out to have had a legal length.
How long was the old Finnish kyynärä?
It was exactly two jalka, Finnish feet of about 29.7 centimetres — the foot was the half, not the kyynärä the double.
It is the field one barrel of seed would sow, about 4,936 square metres — a measure of land defined by its contents.
The kappa survives in Finland for selling potatoes. How many litres is it now?
The old kappa held about 5.5 litres and was rounded down when the metric system came, so the sack shrank slightly.
How many naula made one leiviskä?
Twenty leiviskä made a kippunta of about 170 kilograms, so the whole system ran in twenties rather than tens.
In which year did the metric system become compulsory in Finland?
The law passed in 1886 and the system was merely optional from 1887 — the old units were given six years to die.
How long is a kaapelinmitta, a unit still used at sea?
Its odd-looking figure is simply a tenth of a nautical mile, and the nautical mile is a minute of latitude.
At sea a Finnish syli is 1.852 metres. What does it measure?
It is a thousandth of a nautical mile, so soundings in syli turn into miles with no arithmetic at all.
How many sheets of paper make a riisi?
The old counts sat in several bases at once: a tusina was twelve, a krossi 144 — a dozen dozen.
A motti is a unit of firewood. How much is it?
Three and a half cubic metres
Loose goods each kept their own metric unit: the hehto of a hundred litres did the same job for potatoes.
A vakomitta of about 214 metres was the length of what?
The plough set the unit: how far an ox team would walk before it had to be turned around.
Which of these is an official public holiday in Finland?
Christmas Eve is the day most Finns care about most, and it is not an official holiday at all — only a custom.
Between 1973 and 1991, Finnish Epiphany was moved to which day?
Ascension Day was shifted the same way in the same reform, and both were put back when it proved unpopular.
How many days after Easter Sunday does Helatorstai, Ascension Day, fall?
Forty days counting Easter itself, which is why it is always a Thursday however the date of Easter moves.
How many days after Easter Sunday does Helluntaipäivä, Pentecost, fall?
Seven weeks exactly, which is why the Greek name counts to the fiftieth day with Easter included.
Why does Finnish Midsummer Day move from year to year?
It was tied to a Saturday in 1955
It was fixed at 24 June until 1955, when it was loosened onto the Saturday between the 20th and the 26th.
Pyhäinpäivä, All Saints' Day, falls on the Saturday between which two dates?
It too was fixed, at 1 November, until the 1955 reform swept both it and Midsummer onto Saturdays.
Which three Finnish public holidays are also official flag days?
May Day, Midsummer Day and Independence Day
New Year's Day, May Day and Christmas Day
Easter, May Day and Independence Day
Midsummer Day doubles as the Day of the Finnish Flag, which is why the flag is left up through the night.
Which of Finland's public holidays are not Christian in origin?
Independence Day and All Saints' Day
Only two of the fifteen; even Midsummer, for all its bonfires, arrives in the calendar as St John's day.
Which date is Åland's Autonomy Day?
It is a paid day off only for people working in the public sector, so the shops stay open around them.
Why did Saturdays become days off in Finland?
The working week was cut to 40 hours in the late 1960s
Saturday has never been made an official holiday; it simply behaves like one and always has since.
Mikael Agricola's Day on 9 April is also which day?
The Day of the Finnish Language
The Day of Poetry and Summer
Four writers hold four flag days, and each carries a different cause: language, literature, heritage, poetry.
J. V. Snellman's Day on 12 May is also which day?
The Day of the Finnish Language
He argued Finnish into use as a language of government, so his day is about the nation rather than the tongue.
Minna Canth's Day on 19 March is also which day?
She was the first Finnish woman to be given a flag day of her own, and the cause was attached later.
Miina Sillanpää's Day on 1 October is also which day?
She was Finland's first woman government minister, which is why her day is about taking part rather than about her.
What is 6 November called in Finland?
It is also Gustav Adolf's Day, and the Swedish-speaking Finns are the only language group with a flag day.
Which date is the Finnish Defence Forces Flag Day?
Finland keeps three military or wartime flag days: this one, the veterans' day in April and Remembrance Sunday in May.
Who keeps the Finnish name day calendar?
Its Almanac Office holds a centuries-old printing privilege and sends the list to every calendar publisher.
How often is the Finnish name day list renewed?
Names are added and dropped by how common they have become, so the calendar slowly follows the nursery.
Where was the first almanac in Finnish printed, and when?
Helsinki was then a small coastal town; Turku held the university, the diocese and the printing press.
The Finnish name day calendar grew out of which medieval list?
The calendar of saints of the Diocese of Turku
That is why so many Finnish name days still sit exactly where a saint's feast used to be.
Which name day reform added more than two hundred Finnish names at once?
Until then the calendar was almost entirely Swedish and biblical, so the change was a national argument won.
Besides people, which animals have name days in the Finnish almanac?
The dog calendar runs to 659 names, the cat to 593 and the horse to 590 — more names than many human lists.
Finland's Saami name day calendar was compiled in 1997. What has happened to it since?
Nothing — it has never been revised
It is renewed every five years
It was merged into the Finnish list
It holds 566 names and stands exactly as it was written, while the Finnish list has been reworked six times.
A British rump steak and an American sirloin are the same cut. So what is a British sirloin?
The two vocabularies are crossed over, which is how a menu can promise one steak and bring another.
Which cut of beef gives filet mignon, tournedos and the heart of a beef Wellington?
One muscle, three famous dishes: it does almost no work in the living animal, which is why it is so tender.
The British call the tenderloin fillet. What do the Dutch call it?
The Argentinians call the same muscle lomo — every beef-eating country has named it and none agree.
Which cut of beef becomes both corned beef and pastrami?
It is the same forequarter slab that American barbecue smokes for twelve hours — a tough cut three cuisines rescued.
The Argentine cut bife de chorizo is which steak?
It comes out of the short loin, the primal that also yields the T-bone and the porterhouse from the same bone.
The Brazilian picanha is the fat-capped top of which cut?
It is grilled with the cap left on so the melting fat bastes the meat, which is why it is cut as a thick curved slab.
A beef animal carries two skirts. Where are they?
One on the plate, one on the flank
One on the chuck, one on the round
The outside skirt is the better of the two, and both are the cuts that fill a fajita.
Why does shank beef suit a long-simmered soup so well?
Its connective tissue melts into gelatine
The toughness is the point: the collagen that makes it chewy is exactly what thickens the broth.
Besides the strip, which cut does a T-bone steak contain?
The bone between them is a vertebra, so the steak can only be cut from the short loin and nowhere else.
How many primal cuts is a beef carcass divided into?
Round, loin, rib, chuck, plate, brisket and foreshank — lamb manages with four and veal with four.
Which of these is a primal cut of pork?
The pork primals are ham, loin, Boston butt, picnic and belly with the spare ribs — none of the beef words fit.
Hotel rack is a primal cut of which animal?
Veal is divided into just four: legs, loin, hotel rack and square-cut chuck.
Fatback is a primal pork cut in Europe. What is it in North America?
The same piece of the same animal is a named cut on one continent and a leftover on the other.
The French cut hampe is which steak?
It hangs from the diaphragm, which is where the English name comes from and why there is only one per animal.
Which cut of beef is lean, moderately tough and barely marbled?
It needs either moist cooking or very rare cooking: there is no fat in it to forgive a mistake.
What does PCV stand for on a car engine?
Its valve lets blow-by gases out of the crankcase and back into the intake instead of out into the air.
What does EGR stand for on a car?
The valve feeds a little spent exhaust back into the intake, which cools the burn and cuts nitrogen oxides.
A car's fuel vapour canister has a second, more revealing name. What is it?
It is filled with activated charcoal to trap petrol fumes from the tank until the engine can burn them.
In a drum brake, the wheel cylinder goes by which other name?
The master cylinder at the pedal pushes the fluid; the slave at the wheel obeys it, which is where the names come from.
A car's front spoiler has a plainer name that says what it does. What is it?
It dams the air away from under the car; the one at the back is called a wing instead.
A car's prop shaft is better known by which name?
Short for propeller shaft: the same word a ship uses for the bar between engine and screw.
A Panhard rod belongs to which system of a car?
It is the sideways bar that stops a live axle wandering left and right, and it is named after the carmaker.
A pitman arm belongs to which system of a car?
